title: Gastric Physiology and Function
subject: Physiology
summary: The stomach secretes acid and enzymes to digest food and protect against pathogens. Its function is regulated by nerves and hormones, and impaired function can lead to various gastrointestinal disorders.

sections.p: The stomach is a J-shaped organ that receives food from the oesophagus, mixes it with digestive juices, and empties its contents into the small intestine. It plays a crucial role in digestion and nutrient absorption.

The stomach lining contains glands that secrete gastric juice, a mixture of hydrochloric acid (HCl), pepsinogen, mucus, and intrinsic factor. HCl creates an acidic environment (pH 1.5-3.5) optimal for pepsin activity and kills ingested microbes. Pepsinogen is converted to pepsin, an enzyme that begins protein digestion. Mucus protects the stomach lining from acid and pepsin. Intrinsic factor is essential for vitamin B12 absorption.

Gastric function is regulated by the nervous system (vagus nerve) and hormones. The cephalic phase (sight, smell, taste of food) stimulates secretion. The gastric phase (food in stomach) triggers further secretion via local reflexes and gastrin release. The intestinal phase (food in duodenum) inhibits gastric secretion.
b: Vagus nerve stimulates acid and pepsin secretion.
Secretin and CCK inhibit gastric emptying and secretion.

sections.p: Impaired gastric function can manifest as hypochlorhydria (low acid), achlorhydria (no acid), or hyperchlorhydria (high acid). This can result from infections (e.g., Helicobacter pylori), autoimmune conditions (pernicious anaemia), chronic gastritis, or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Reduced acid can impair digestion and increase infection risk, while excess acid can damage the mucosa.
b: Reduced acid: malabsorption, increased infection risk.
Increased acid: peptic ulcer disease, gastritis.

sections.p: Understanding gastric function is vital for diagnosing and managing conditions like peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, malabsorption syndromes (e.g., vitamin B12 deficiency), and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. In low-resource settings, infections like H. pylori and parasitic infestations are common causes of gastric complaints.

t.b: What symptoms suggest a gastric problem? (e.g., dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, bleeding)
What signs might be present? (e.g., epigastric tenderness, signs of anaemia, dehydration)

sections.p: Examiners will assess your understanding of how gastric secretions and motility are regulated, and how disruptions lead to common clinical problems.

t.b: What is the role of HCl? — Kills microbes, denatures proteins, activates pepsinogen.
What does pepsin do? — Initiates protein digestion.
How is the stomach lining protected? — Mucus layer, bicarbonate secretion, rapid cell turnover.
What stimulates gastric acid? — Vagus nerve (acetylcholine), gastrin, histamine.
How does H. pylori affect gastric function? — Causes inflammation, reduces acid in some cases, increases risk of ulcers and cancer.
What is the link between pernicious anaemia and gastric function? — Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells leads to achlorhydria and B12 malabsorption.
What factors affect gastric emptying? — Volume, composition of meal, hormones (CCK), neural input.
A patient presents with epigastric pain relieved by food. What is the likely diagnosis and why? — Duodenal ulcer. Acid production is high, food buffers acid temporarily.

faq.q: What is the main function of stomach acid?
faq.a: To kill ingested microorganisms and create an optimal pH for pepsin to digest proteins.

faq.q: What is intrinsic factor and why is it important?
faq.a: Intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells and is essential for the absorption of vitamin B12 in the ileum.

faq.q: How can H. pylori affect gastric function?
faq.a: H. pylori infection causes chronic inflammation (gastritis), which can impair acid secretion and increase the risk of peptic ulcers and gastric cancer.
